scenario: The data-centre lease ends in fourteen months. Dev proposes rewriting every application as cloud-native services before moving anything.
options: Rewrite everything first; it saves moving twice
Choose a strategy per workload - retire, retain, rehost, replatform where cheap - migrate first, and modernise the valuable systems afterwards
Rehost everything and never change it
Extend the lease indefinitely
explanation: Rewrites are where exits miss their dates. Migrating first meets the deadline; replatforming where it is cheap and modernising afterwards captures the benefits without betting the date on them.

stem: Why should Azure Migrate discovery run for several weeks before sizing decisions are made?
options: The appliance needs weeks to install
Microsoft requires it
Performance-based sizing needs real utilisation across normal cycles - month-end, peaks - and dependency analysis needs time to see every connection
Discovery is free only after a month
explanation: Sizing from the on-site specification copies years of over-provisioning, and a week of data misses month-end jobs. Weeks of data give right-sized targets and a complete dependency map.

scenario: After cutover, the order system fails every morning at 06:00. It turns out to call a licence server that is still on site and was not in any plan.
options: Dependency analysis during discovery, grouping the licence server into the same wave
A larger VM in Azure
Moving the order system first on its own
A longer hypercare period
explanation: Dependency data shows who talks to whom from real traffic, including rare scheduled calls, so dependent servers move together. Hypercare only finds the problem after it has happened.

stem: Which sequence describes a sound cutover for a workload?
options: Copy it on Friday night and switch DNS
Rewrite it, then deploy
Move every workload the same weekend
Replicate, test-migrate into an isolated network with the app owner's sign-off, cut over in an agreed window with go/no-go criteria and a rollback plan, hypercare, then decommission
explanation: Each step reduces risk: test migration proves the app works in Azure, the rollback plan bounds the downside, and decommissioning stops you paying for two estates.

scenario: The old order-management monolith has moved to Azure unchanged. The team wants to modernise it without a risky big-bang replacement.
options: Strangler fig: put a façade such as API Management in front, rebuild one capability at a time as a new service, and switch its route - rollback is a routing change
Freeze all changes until a full rewrite is ready
Copy the monolith into microservices line by line
Move it back on site
explanation: The strangler fig delivers value incrementally and keeps each step reversible. Full rewrites carry all the risk at the end and usually overrun.

scenario: Warehouse systems must stay on site for latency and to keep working when the internet link drops. Security wants them patched, monitored and governed like everything in Azure.
options: Rehosting them to Azure anyway
Azure Arc: the servers appear in Azure and get Azure Policy, Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor and update management
A separate on-site tool for each concern
A site-to-site VPN only
explanation: Arc brings non-Azure servers under the same management plane. A VPN connects networks but governs nothing, and rehosting ignores the reason they stay.

scenario: Three months after rehosting 80 VMs, the Azure bill is higher than the data centre's running costs.
stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Azure is always more expensive; accept it
Move everything to Kubernetes
VMs were sized from the on-site specifications; right-size from real utilisation, apply Azure Hybrid Benefit, buy reservations for the steady baseline, and switch off the old servers
Turn off monitoring
explanation: Lift and shift copies over-provisioning. Right-sizing, existing licences, commitments on proven usage and decommissioning the source are what make the migration cheaper.

scenario: Twenty-two SQL Server instances use SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries heavily.
stem: Which target is the sensible replatform?
options: Cosmos DB
Azure SQL Database single databases, rewriting the jobs first
SQL Server on VMs, one per instance, unchanged
Azure SQL Managed Instance, consolidating instances, moved with the Database Migration Service or the Managed Instance link
explanation: Managed Instance keeps instance-level features such as SQL Agent and cross-database queries while removing the patching and backups. SQL Database would need rework first, and VMs keep all the operational work.
